passages.text: Going local: Evaluating guideline adherence and appropriateness of antibiotic prescribing in patients with febrile neutropenia at an academic teaching hospital
Background:

Febrile neutropenia (FN) is a medical emergency with significant morbidity and mortality for oncology patients, requiring comprehensive workup and timely antibiotic administration. We evaluated concordance with locally developed FN guidelines and outcomes of cancer patients admitted to general internal medicine at an academic teaching hospital.
Methods:

We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study of patients admitted between July 1, 2016, and June 30, 2017, for FN. Patients were classified as having low-risk or high-risk FN according to their malignancy and chemotherapy. Primary outcome was the proportion of patients receiving guideline-concordant antibiotics within 48 hours of admission to general internal medicine. Secondary outcomes were the proportion of patients in whom empirical antibiotics were active against pathogens isolated, rate of antibiotic-associated adverse events, and in-hospital mortality. We used logistic regression to model relationship between FN risk and guideline-concordant antibiotics.
Results:

Among 100 patients included, 34 (34%) were low-risk FN and 66 (66%) were high-risk. Proportion of guideline-concordant empirical antibiotics was significantly lower among low-risk FN patients than high-risk patients: 12 (35%) of 34 versus 47 (71%) of 66 (P = .001). Empirical antibiotics were active against 17 (94%) of 18 isolated pathogens. The mortality rate was 3%, and 16% of patients experienced antibiotic-associated adverse events. Hematological malignancy and infectious diseases-trained physician involvement were associated with guideline-concordant prescribing, with adjusted odds ratios of 3.76 (95% CI, 1.46-9.70; P = .006) and 3.71 (95% CI, 1.49-9.23; P = .005), respectively.
Conclusions:
Guideline concordance was low compared to published reports. Factors influencing appropriate antimicrobial prescribing in patients with FN warrant further exploration.

Febrile neutropenia (FN) is a medical emergency associated with significant potential morbidity and mortality for oncology patients.   Signs and symptoms of infection are often absent or ambiguous due to diminished inflammatory responses in this patient population, but given the risk of infectious complications, timely administration of empirical antibiotics is recommended.   The guideline from the Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) for antimicrobial stewardship programs (ASP) has highlighted the value of ASP interventions in oncology patients to ensure appropriate selection of antibiotics tailored to local epidemiology while reducing antibiotic-associated adverse events associated with inappropriate use.   The IDSA has emphasized the role of facility-specific, locally developed FN guidelines in this patient population.   The implementation of institutional FN guidelines can help to optimize patient care by promoting best practices, improving patient outcomes, and reducing costs.

The University Health Network (UHN) is a tertiary academic teaching hospital system affiliated with the University of Toronto. It includes 3 acute-care sites: Toronto General Hospital (TG), Princess Margaret Cancer Centre (PM), and Toronto Western Hospital. The UHN ASP created 2 FN guidelines based on local susceptibility pattern, patient population, and resources.   One guideline is specific for patients with hematological malignancies such as acute leukemia and recipients of stem-cell transplant pre-engraftment, who are at high risk for infectious complications.   The other guideline is specific for patients undergoing treatment for solid tumor, who are considered to be at low risk of infectious complications.   The guideline for patients with hematological malignancies or stem-cell transplant recommends piperacillin-tazobactam plus tobramycin as empiric antimicrobial therapy. The guideline for the solid-tumor patients recommends cefazolin plus tobramycin. Empirical tobramycin is limited to a maximum of 72 hours for both guidelines while microbiological investigations are pending and diagnostic workup are underway. The inclusion of tobramycin is to ensure adequate gram-negative coverage, reflecting the epidemiology from the PM-specific antibiograms and Public Health Ontario's provincial report. The prevalence of multidrug-resistant gram-negative rods in blood isolates is estimated to be between 20% and 25% in the local patient population.   Meropenem is the empirical alternative for patients with self-reported allergy to penicillin and those with history of colonization or infection due to extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing gram-negative bacilli.

In this study, we evaluated concordance with the FN guidelines and appropriateness of antibiotic prescribing among cancer patients admitted to TG general internal medicine (GIM) service. Although PM specializes in treating complex cancer patients, those who experience infectious complications are commonly admitted to TG. We aimed to identify opportunities to optimize febrile neutropenia management in GIM through this quality improvement initiative.
Methods
Design, setting, and study population

We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study of patients admitted to GIM between July 2016 and June 2017. The GIM service consisted of between 60 and 65 beds. Patients were identified by the UHN Department of Clinical Decision Support. We included patients with a primary discharge diagnosis of first-episode FN based on the International Classification of Disease, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) codes, who had a current oncology diagnosis and were currently receiving chemotherapy within 6 months prior to admission. We included patients admitted from TG emergency department or from PM's rapid assessment clinic (TG and PM are located on the same street, across from one another). Patients were excluded if they were hematopoietic stem-cell transplant recipients in the postengraftment phase or if they were not undergoing chemotherapy. The study was approved by the UHN Institutional Review Board.
Intervention

No direct antimicrobial stewardship interventions were underway in GIM during the study period. Following the launch of the FN guidelines (version 2016), presentations to introduce the guidelines were given by the ASP team to clinical teams across the UHN, including the TG GIM program. The guidelines are available on the institution's intranet and on the ASP website.
Data collection

Following eligible patients identified by the clinical decision support team, baseline patient demographics, clinical parameters including neutrophil counts and documented fever, imaging studies and microbiology data were collected through manual review of the institution's electronic health record (EHR) system. An antimicrobial stewardship report generated by the ASP was provided to record the antibiotic regimens used.
Definitions

FN was defined as per the IDSA guideline, with a composite of neutropenia as an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of <=0.5 x 109/L or an ANC that is anticipated to decrease to <0.5 x 109/L during the following 48 hours. Fever was defined as any reported or measured temperature of >=38.3 C once or sustained temperature of >=38 C for at least 1 hour.   Oncology diagnoses were classified as follows: active solid tumor included breast, lung, colorectal, other gastrointestinal, gynecologic, genitourinary, head and neck, and low-risk lymphoma; active hematological malignancy included acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), mixed ALL and AML, high-grade lymphoma (e.g., diffuse large B-cell lymphoma), chronic lymphoblastic leukemia (CLL), multiple myeloma, and myelodysplastic syndrome.   We stratified patients as having low-risk or high-risk FN based on the IDSA guidelines, which were adopted in the UHN guidelines in 2014 and first updated in 2016. Low-risk patients were expected to have a short neutropenic period of <=7 days; high-risk patients were anticipated to have prolonged neutropenia of >7 days; and profound neutropenia was defined as an absolute neutrophil count <=0.1 x 109 cells/L. In practice, patients undergoing treatment for solid tumor were managed under the low-risk guideline and patients with hematological malignancies were managed under the high-risk guideline. Age was categorized into <65 years or >=65 years.

Guideline concordance was defined as the prescription of an empirical antimicrobial regimen that was consistent with the UHN FN guidelines recommendation according to the risk stratification of the patient. Empirical antimicrobials were considered appropriate if the regimen was active against the pathogen isolated from a microbiological culture and/or appropriate for the source of infection (e.g., pneumonia) according to the indication in the medical records. Antibiotic-associated adverse events were defined according to Tamma et al.   Adverse events reported during hospitalization were categorized by body systems: gastrointestinal, dermatologic, musculoskeletal, hematologic, hepatobiliary, renal, cardiac, and/or neurologic.

Appropriateness of antimicrobial and guideline concordance were adjudicated by a study investigator (R.L.). For quality assurance, another clinician independently audited 20 randomly selected charts for accuracy of data collection.
Outcomes

The primary outcome was the proportion of patients who received guideline-concordant antimicrobials within 48 hours of admission to GIM. We excluded antimicrobials administered while patients were in the emergency department because they had not been officially under the care of the attending internists. Secondary outcomes evaluated whether empirical antibiotics were active against the isolated pathogen or appropriate for the source of infection, factors associated with guideline concordance, incidence of nosocomial Clostridioides difficile infection, antibiotic-associated adverse events, length of stay under the GIM service, and in-hospital all-cause mortality.
Statistical analysis

Baseline characteristics were reported with descriptive statistics. Outcome measures were compared using the chi2 test for categorical variables and the Wilcoxon rank-sum test for continuous variables. Univariable and multivariable logistic regression models were used to assess the association between FN risk and receipt of guideline-concordant antibiotics, adjusting for age, sex, type of cancer (e.g., hematological malignancy vs. solid tumor), and infectious diseases (ID) physician involvement. ID involvement was defined as having received ID specialist consultation or being under the care of an attending internist who was also a qualified ID consultant. Odds ratios (OR) and adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the primary outcome were reported. Model goodness-of-fit was assessed with the Akaike information criterion and likelihood ratio test. We defined P < .05 as statistically significant. Statistical analysis was completed using STATA version 16.0 software (StataCorp, College Station, TX).
Results
Patient demographics and clinical characteristics

In total, 100 patients met eligibility criteria to be included in the study. Baseline characteristics are presented in Table 1. Among them, 34 (34%) had low-risk FN and 66 (66%) patients had high-risk FN. Among the low-risk patients, duration of neutropenia was <7 days in 30 (88.2%) of 34 patients, although 15 (44%) had an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) of <=0.1 x 109 cells/L. In the high-risk group, 73% had ANC <=0.1 x109 cells/L and 11% had neutropenia lasting 7 days or longer. Length of stay (LOS) was longer in the high-risk group (median, 6 days; interquartile range [IQR], 5) than the low-risk group (median 4, IQR 5; P = .0424). Duration of fever was shorter in the low-risk group, with a mean of 1.1 days (standard deviation, +-0.9 days), compared to 2.2 days (+-1.9) in the high-risk group (P = .002).

Primary outcome

All patients received antimicrobials within 48 hours of admission to GIM. Overall, the antimicrobial management of 59 (59%) of 100 patients was guideline concordant. In the low-risk group, 12 (35%) of 34 patients received guideline-concordant antimicrobials, and in the high-risk group 47 (71%) of 66 received guideline-concordant antimicrobials (P = .001) (Table 2). Patients in the low-risk group were less likely to have ID involvement compared to the high-risk group: 14 (41%) of 34 versus 43 (65%) of 66, respectively (P = .022). Factors associated with receiving guideline-concordant antimicrobials included type of cancer (hematological malignancy or pre-engraftment following stem-cell transplant versus solid tumor (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 3.76; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.46-9.70; P = .006) and involvement by an ID physician (aOR, 3.71; 95% CI, 1.49-9.23; P = .005) (Table 3).

Regarding guideline-discordant antimicrobials received within the first 48 hours of admission to GIM, 9 (26%) of 34 patients in the low-risk group received piperacillin-tazobactam and tobramycin empirically, and 6 (18%) of 34 received piperacillin-tazobactam monotherapy, instead of cefazolin and tobramycin as recommended by the local guideline. In the high-risk group, 8 (12%) of 66 received piperacillin-tazobactam monotherapy, rather than piperacillin-tazobactam plus tobramycin as recommended by the local guideline.
Secondary outcomes

Source of infection was identified in 50% of patients. The cause of fever was not identified in the other half of the study population. Of the 22 microbiologically defined infections, empiric antibiotic regimens were active against 17 (94%) of 18 bacterial pathogens isolated. Of the pathogens isolated, 8 of 22 were from blood specimens: 3 were gram-negative bacilli, 3 were gram-positive cocci, and 2 were polymicrobial. Of the 14 nonblood isolates, 7 were from urine specimens, all of which were gram-negative bacilli. Several multidrug-resistant organisms were identified. One vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE) and 1 extended-spectrum beta-lactamase-producing (ESBL) Escherischia coli were isolated from a blood and urine source, respectively. Clinically defined infections occurred in 28 (28%) of 100 patients. Pneumonia was diagnosed in 21 patients, and 7 had skin and soft-tissue infections.

Hospital-onset of C. difficile infection occurred in 4 (4%) of 100. In-hospital all-cause mortality occurred in 3 (3%) of 100. Antibiotic-associated adverse drug events occurring in 16 (16%) of 100 patients with the most common being non-C. difficile associated diarrhea (n = 9), followed by dermatologic reaction (n = 3), and 1 patient each with hepatobiliary, gastrointestinal, renal, and neurological adverse events.
Discussion

At our institution, the overall guideline concordance among FN patients in GIM at the Toronto General Hospital was low at 59%. Concordance was higher in the high-risk group (71%) than in the low-risk group (35%). Overall, guideline-concordant empirical antimicrobials were active against the clinical syndromes and isolated pathogens in FN patients, except for 1 VRE infection. A point-prevalence audit conducted at Princess Margaret Cancer Center in 2017 found FN guideline concordance to be 73% in patients with acute leukemia. The practice model and staffing at the malignant hematology units differed from that in the GIM units at Toronto General Hospital, which are clinical teaching units and patient care is provided by learners at various stages of training under the direct supervision of the attending internists. Furthermore, the ASP team conducted twice-weekly audit-and-feedback in the malignant hematology units at Princess Margaret. However, in TG GIM units, no direct antimicrobial stewardship interventions were conducted.

Our guideline-concordant antimicrobial prescribing was lower than the 79% reported in a database study of admission records between 2000 and 2010.   However, our results shared common patterns with contemporaneous reports. Guideline concordance was 85.4% in a series of point-prevalence surveys conducted between 2014 and 2018 in a combination of academic and community hospitals in Australia.   In this cohort, hematology patients were more likely to receive antimicrobials concordant with local guidelines than solid-tumor patients.   Baugh et al   conducted a case-vignettes survey among 107 oncologists of an academic cancer center and 44 physicians from the emergency department (ED) of an affiliated teaching hospital in 2015. These researchers reported that 96% of oncologists and 100% of ED physicians selected guideline-concordant antimicrobials for high-risk patients but that only 61% of oncologists and 23% of ED physicians selected appropriate plans for low-risk patients.   In a retrospective cohort study by the same authors, guideline concordance was 70% among patients who presented with FN to the ED in 2010-2014, including 44 low-risk and 129 high-risk visits.   There was a significant difference in the prevalence of guideline-discordant antimicrobials between low-risk and high-risk patients (98% vs 7%; risk ratio, 14; 95% CI, 7.5-26).   Schuttevaer et al   reported guideline adherence to be 395 (43.5%) of 909 in a retrospective cohort of FN patients who presented to the ED at a tertiary-care university hospital and had bloodstream infections between 2012 and 2017.   In this study, over-treatment (spectrum too broad) with empirical antibiotics was not associated with survival benefit.

Several factors may have contributed to poor guideline compliance in GIM. First, there were barriers to effective communication. UHN had a hybrid system of paper chart plus EHR that was not integrated with venues of communication, mainly paging and e-mail. GIM patients were located in several units, which were physical barriers of communication between prescribers and the ASP team. In addition, the GIM program is located at Toronto General Hospital:a different building from the Princess Margaret Cancer Centre:and did not receive scheduled audit-and-feedback interventions from the ASP team. No GIM pharmacist was dedicated to reviewing antimicrobial management in oncology patients or to liaising with the ASP team.

Second, there appeared to be a lack of familiarity of the FN guidelines among the GIM teams. Although the guidelines were on our institution's intranet and the ASP website, active implementation strategies, education, and promotion efforts were not sustained in GIM units. In the survey conducted by Baugh et al   in 2015, only 54% of oncologists and 26% of ED physicians were familiar with the IDSA guideline.   Unfamiliarity with the guideline was associated with unnecessary empirical vancomycin in high-risk patients.   In the Australian point-prevalence surveys, among hematology patients, 20.2% of meropenem and 11.3% of vancomycin were adjudicated as spectrum being too broad.   In our study, the most common guideline-discordant prescribing in low-risk patients was the spectrum being too broad. Piperacillin-tazobactam monotherapy or in combination with tobramycin were prescribed instead of cefazolin and tobramycin. Because our recommended empirical therapy differed from the international guidelines, prescribers were not familiar with the rationale based on local epidemiology.   Concerns regarding ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity from tobramycin exposure, albeit for <=72 hours, may have contributed to a reluctance to prescribe.

Lastly, cancer type and ID physician involvement (as the primary team physician or formal consultation service) were independently associated with guideline-concordant antimicrobials. ID physicians may be more familiar with the guidelines, whereas patients with hematological malignancies were more likely to receive ID consultation service.   Conversely, as demonstrated by Douglas et al,   solid-tumor patients may have less exposure to oversight by ID specialists and ASP interventions. ID specialist involvement may promote guideline-driven practice by raising the awareness of other clinicians toward them.

Since the conclusion of this study, TG GIM has installed a clinical pharmacist for oncology patients, who liaises with the ASP team and ID consultants. Recently, UHN replaced the hybrid system of paper chart and EHR system with an enterprise-wide integrated EHR system. The new system has built-in communication tools, documentation, and clinical decision support. Clinicians can access information on patients' current cancer therapy directly. We anticipate that the new system will facilitate guideline-based prescribing and will improve the efficiency of evaluating prescribing practice.   We are upgrading our guidelines to reflect a more nuanced approach to risk stratification, accounting for cancer diagnosis and up-to-date treatment.

The strengths of our study were intertwined with the quality improvement process. First, we focused on evaluating concordance and outcomes of patients admitted to GIM for FN, whereas many recent publications have concentrated on patients presented to the ED.   Second, beyond process measures, we assessed appropriateness of guideline-recommended antimicrobials in the initial 48 hours after admission and clinical outcomes based on microbiological investigations. In comparison, others have focused on evaluating a single agent, most commonly vancomycin,   route of antimicrobial administration,   or admission according to disease burden score.   There is increasing emphasis on auditing adherence to guidelines by standards-setting organizations such as the Center for Disease Control and the Joint Commission.   In an era with growing prevalence of multidrug-resistant organisms, receiving inappropriate empirical antimicrobial treatment is associated with morbidity and mortality.   Third, in our study population, patients were admitted over a 1-year period after guideline implementation. These results reflect the validity of the guideline recommendations. Previous publications have reported on data for cohorts of patients accumulated over long periods, often upwards of 5 years. The validity of those guidelines may wane over time owing to changes in the epidemiology of infectious complications, antimicrobial resistance, and advances in cancer treatment.

Our study had several limitations. First, given its retrospective nature, the accuracy and validity of the data were limited by the quality of the documentation. A detailed examination of the prescriber's clinical reasoning was precluded because the rationale and thought process behind antimicrobial prescribing was infrequently recorded. Second, there was overlap in duration and nadir of neutropenia between the high-risk and low-risk groups, suggesting that risk differentiation can be improved by incorporating details of cancer diagnosis and treatment. Third, as a single-center study, local factors contributing to guideline discordance may not apply elsewhere.

Further studies with quantitative and qualitative methods are needed to better understand why prescribers are not compliant with FN guideline recommendations and how those barriers can be removed.   Serial point-prevalence audits on guidelines concordance and appropriateness of antimicrobial prescribing using an a priori adjudication framework with prescriber-specific data may be useful.   In conclusion, we demonstrated that after developing local FN guidelines and making them available to prescribers, maintaining antimicrobial stewardship efforts, giving feedback, and evaluating adherence are imperative to ensuring that prescribers use antimicrobials according to best practices.

passages.text: Nurse Engagement in Antibiotic Stewardship Programs: A Scoping Review of the Literature
Introduction:

Hospital-based antibiotic stewardship programs (ASPs) are an important strategy in combating antibiotic resistance. Four antibiotic stewardship interventions are recommended by the CDC as particularly well-designed to engage nurses. However, there is limited information on whether and how existing hospital-based ASPs reflect these practices.
Purpose:
To describe how nurses are being engaged in hospital ASPs and to what extent this overlaps with the CDC framework.
Methods:
This scoping review included studies published in the last ten years on engaging nurses in hospital-based ASPs. Three databases, PubMed, CINAHL, and Embase, were searched.
Results:

The search yielded 195 unique manuscripts. Ten manuscripts were retained for review detailing how nurses are engaged. One CDC recommended intervention, initiating discussion of antibiotic treatment, appeared in nine studies.
Conclusions:

While hospitals are engaging nurses in antibiotic stewardship programs, their selected approaches do not reflect the full breadth of the opportunities identified by the CDC. More detail as to how exactly nurses engage would also be a useful addition to the literature.
Implications:

More research is needed on nurse engagement on culturing/testing and penicillin allergy evaluation. Standardized measures should be collected and reported to measure the impact of engaging nurses in ASPs.
INTRODUCTION

Health care across the world has entered a post-antibiotic era; people are dying from infections because some organisms have become resistant to antibiotics. In 2019, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimated that over 2.8 million antibiotic resistant infections occur in the US each year, resulting in more than 35,000 deaths. In Europe, 33,000 people die from antibiotic resistant infections annually as of 2018. Estimates also suggest as of 2011 that the annual economic burden of these infections is $55 billion in the US, $1.5 billion yearly in the European Union, and is projected to impose a total burden of $100 trillion globally by 2050 if improvements are not made.

Antibiotic stewardship programs (ASPs) have emerged as one strategy to decrease the burden of antibiotic resistant infections. ASPs target the appropriate use of antibiotics, including preventing overuse, through multi-level, multi-disciplinary action. In 2015, CDC's National Action Plan for Combating Antibiotic-Resistant Bacteria called for the establishment of ASPs in all acute care hospitals by 2020, naming eight Core Elements for inclusion - hospital leadership commitment, accountability, pharmacy expertise, action, tracking, reporting, education, and CDC support. As of 2018, 85% of acute care hospitals in the US reported having all CDC Core Elements for ASPs in place.

In US hospitals, nursing comprises the largest sector of the workforce accounting for 30% of employees worldwide and the largest occupational group in the health sector, accounting for approximately 59% of the health professions. As such, the potential impact of nurses to play critical roles in multidisciplinary ASPs is evident. In a 2018 study of inpatient staff nurses, 69.4% of nurses understood what the term "antibiotic stewardship" meant, 54% of nurses perceived that they were already functioning in a stewardship role, and the majority wanted to be more involved in the stewardship process. In 2019, the CDC added a new category of nursing-based actions to the Core Elements for Hospital ASPs to reflect the important role that nurses play. The report identified four opportunities in which hospital leadership may engage nurses in ASPs, including: 1) optimizing testing/diagnostic stewardship [e.g., assessing if a patient might have symptoms that justify a urine culture]; 2) assuring that cultures are performed correctly prior to starting antibiotics; 3) initiating discussions about antibiotic treatment; and 4) improving evaluation of penicillin allergies. Despite this stronger emphasis on the role of nursing in ASPs, little is understood about if, how, and where hospitals are engaging nurses in ASPs to address this global problem. The aim of this scoping review is to describe how and where (both in the US and internationally) nurses are being engaged in hospital ASPs and determine if and how this reported engagement overlaps with the four CDC opportunities.
METHODS

A scoping review was selected as the most appropriate method to address the study aim as nurse-specific guidelines were published recently. A scoping review allows for the authors to undertake a structured approach to identify types of evidence and knowledge gaps in ASPs related to nurse engagement and provide a descriptive account of the available literature. Using this method we will select the studies, chart the data to extract relevant information, collate, summarize and report the results. IRB approval was not required as this study reviews existing literature.
Eligibility Criteria

Eligible studies included peer-reviewed, full-text manuscripts published between January 2011 and March 2021 on original research studies or quality improvement initiatives that included nurses in hospital-based ASPs. We selected this 10-year time period to fully capture articles that may address the study aims before and after the publication of the CDC guidelines (as articles may include an activity prior to the CDC formalization of guidance). Articles with a research purpose solely of defining or reviewing the role of the nurse in ASPs or that did not include engagement initiatives were excluded.

The authors chose not to restrict the definition of "engagement" a priori to allow for a wider breadth of literature to be returned during the search process. Instead, we chose to examine it operationally, using the opportunities for engagement set forth by the CDC - optimizing testing, correct culturing, prompting antibiotic treatment discussions, and penicillin allergy evaluation - as a framework for analysis.
Information Sources

Three databases were utilized: 1) PubMed; 2) CINAHL; and 3) Embase. Authors of abstract-only pieces (conference abstracts) were emailed if contact information was available. Only full-text articles were included in the full-text review. The search strategy was developed in consultation with a research librarian at our institution's health science library. The search strategy was built in a stepwise fashion comparing keywords and their PubMed MeSH counterparts. Boolean operators were added between terms for a final search strategy using key words ("Nursing" OR "Nurse") AND ("Antibiotic Stewardship" OR "Antibiotic Stewardship") AND ("Engagement" OR "Involvement"). The search strategy established in PubMed was then translated to the two other databases.
Selection of Sources of Evidence

After the search was completed in each database, results were exported and uploaded to Covidence (Veritas Health Innovation, 2021) for article management and review. The primary author (CTJ) screened the article titles and abstracts for relevance. Reviewing authors (CTJ and LJR) screened the full text for relevance. All articles then received a vote from each reviewer (CTJ, LJR) to include or exclude from the final review. Any conflicts were resolved through meetings to clarify reasons for exclusion/inclusion and until consensus was reached.

A data extraction and charting tool was designed and pilot tested by two authors using two articles to establish usability and consistency in approach. Subsequently, both reviewers extracted data independently for the remaining articles.
RESULTS
Article Selection and Characteristics

The initial search yielded 265 articles, of those, 70 were duplicates. Following removal of duplicates, 195 article title and abstracts were screened for relevance and 25 studies were included for full-text review. During full-text retrieval, 8 abstract-only pieces were excluded. Following full-text review, 7 articles were excluded because nurse engagement was not explicitly included (4), ASP was not implemented (2), and no intervention was identified (1). This yielded 10 articles for data extraction and charting (Figure 1).

Half of the studies were conducted in the US (n=5) and the remaining in Canada (n=2), Australia (n=1), India (n=1), and Malawi (n=1) (Table 1). All study populations included bedside nurses, with six of the studies targeting bedside and or managerial/charge nurses exclusively. Gillespie et al. focused on experienced nurses, excluding new graduates. Four articles included other clinical personnel - physicians, pharmacists, aides - on the multidisciplinary team in the study. Four of the studies took place in an intensive or critical care setting, two in an emergency or trauma setting, two in a step-down or medical ward, and four articles did not specify the type of units participating in the study.

There was marked heterogeneity in subjects sampled and size. Four studies defined their sample as nurses and specified the number participating, ranging from 13 to 121. Three studies defined their sample to be patients or patient encounters and included the size, ranging from 458 - 867 patients/encounters. One study defined their sample as four multidisciplinary teams totaling 25 members. Two studies defined their sample as the unit in aggregate and did not specify the number of staff or patients making up the analytic sample. Nine out of ten studies  reviewed had a quality improvement design, with three studies describing their design as either experimental or quasi-experimental. One study, Mula et al., employed a qualitative case study design to understand nurse workarounds to stewardship practices.
Synthesis of Results

First, categorical themes were created to chart the methods study authors employed in ASP initiatives: 1) educational; 2) rounding; 3) tool- or algorithm-based; 4) implementation bundle; and 5) discussion/reflection. (Table 1) Three studies employed an education-based intervention to engage nurses in ASPs activities,  two studies reported a rounding intervention to engage nurses,  two centered their intervention on a tool- or algorithm-based care activity cluster,  two studies included implementation bundles of varying size and components,  and one article utilized a practice discussion- and reflection-based approach. Next, the extent and methods that each study addressed one or more of the four CDC opportunities (optimizing testing, performing cultures correctly, initiating discussions about antibiotic treatment, and improving evaluation of penicillin allergies) for nurse engagement were assessed. While most opportunities were represented in at least one article, none of the articles explicitly discussed including accurate assessments of penicillin allergies in their initiatives.
Optimizing Testing

Two studies described initiatives designed to optimize testing techniques and encourage diagnostic stewardship. Fitzpatrick et al. included content on avoiding inappropriate culturing orders. Walters et al. included education and supporting materials to both physicians and nurses on proper ordering of a urinalysis and culture, a "quick pick order list" to narrow ordering down to only urinalysis and culture, and development of "SmartPhrases" to facilitate documentation of collection method.
Performing Cultures Correctly

Three studies included initiatives to assure that cultures are performed correctly and before starting antibiotics. Fitzpatrick et al. provided tips on proper culture techniques and timing to nurses during a 2-hour interactive session. Monsees et al. encouraged nurse investigation into culture results for any patient with antibiotics ordered using education on the reverse side of the "ADIOS Antibiotic Engagement Tool (AET)" and assessed nurse confidence in assuring that cultures are obtained prior to starting antibiotics pre- and post-intervention through surveys. Using a clinical decision support algorithm, Walters et al. addressed correct culturing practices through coaching of nurses on culturing methods for children based on toilet training status and standardized patient education on collecting clean catch specimens.
Initiating Discussions About Antibiotic Treatment

Nine studies reported initiatives for engaging nurses in ASPs by involving them with antibiotic discussions or prompting discussions about antibiotic treatments. The ADIOS AET from Monsees et al. was designed for nurses to use to initiate discussions about antibiotic treatment during care transitions, operationally defined as a transfer of a patient's care between services, a patient admission, and a patient discharge.  Shukla et al. utilized charge nurses to lead nursing-based ASPs and discussions about antibiotic treatment. During charge nurse-led antibiotic timeout "clinical huddles", the charge nurses reviewed antibiotic therapy, provided recommendations and guidelines on antibiotics prescription, promoted shorter antibiotic courses for culture-negative sepsis, and reviewed indications for antibiotic usage in the neonatal intensive care unit. Fitzpatrick et al. educated the nurses on participating in rounds and initiating in antibiotic discussions by and starting antibiotic timeouts.

Ha et al. educated nurses on antibiotic rounding and included coaching and semi-weekly rounding coordination support from a nurse champion as well as an infectious disease pharmacist, infection preventionist, and critical care nurse practioner. Raybardhan et al. also incorporated rounding, focusing on nurse-prompted duration of therapy discussions. The nurses were provided education on antimicrobial reassessment and provided with information on common critical care unit antimicrobials as well as a standard script to introduce duration of therapy discussions during daily rounding.

Verma et al. provided education and guides to nurses on reviewing antibiotic therapy details, policy and how to discuss therapy with the treating physician. Similarly, Gillespie et al. aimed two annual "switch to oral" educational sessions at empowering nurses to influence antibiotic management, and to question medical staff about the need for continued antibiotic use in each patient. Jeffs et al. educated four implementation teams on QI methods, collaboratives, Communities of Practice, and insights from previous literature on ASPs. The implementation teams focused on initiatives to improving communication around antibiotic therapy changes and appropriateness and debriefed to evaluate themes of success. Mula et al. used direct observation of nurse practices by other medical team members around four types of antibiotic management encounters - nurses' shift change handover reports, antibiotic preparation, antibiotic administration, and ward rounds. After data collection, the researchers held focus groups with team members and purposive interviews with nurses for feedback, reflection and discussion on antibiotic workarounds.

Finally, we examined how the different interventions described in the literature overlap with the CDC opportunities for nursing engagement in ASPs (Figure 3). We found that interventions that utilized an education or tool-based intervention included more than one engagement opportunity whereas other intervention approaches (rounding, bundles, and discussion) focused on a singular opportunity to engage nurses in ASPs.

We also found that the outcomes that researchers used to evaluate the effectiveness of their interventions varied widely. Four studies focused on more subjective outcomes such as pre/post intervention surveys or guided interview themes. Five looked at objective outcomes such as IV line days, healthcare-associated infections, duration of therapy, charting/order patterns, and length of stay.. The only article to combine both subjective self-report data and objective aggregate care outcome statistics in a mixed-methods approach was that by Gillespie et al. (Table 1).
LIMITATIONS

As this scoping review included peer-reviewed literature only, it is possible some quality improvement initiatives have been reported outside of the peer-reviewed literature, thus selection bias may exist. In addition, an inherent limitation of scoping review methodology is the absence of formal study quality appraisal as the intent is to gather information from a broad range of study designs. Finally, while the CDC participates in global antibiotic resistance initiatives and contributes to standards beyond US borders, we recognize that they are a US-based agency and the opportunities for engagement might not reflect practice in hospital settings outside of the US.
DISCUSSION

This scoping review provides an overview of the available evidence to answer the questions "how are nurses being engaged in hospital ASPs?" and "do these strategies target or include CDC opportunities for nurse engagement?" The available evidence suggests a growing focus on antibiotic stewardship as an important target of quality improvement programming and global interest in engaging nurses in ASPs.

A disappointing finding was the inclusion and description of nurse involvement in ASPs. Multi-disciplinary articles that were included in this review tended to have limited information on the extent of nurse involvement in the APSs and/or included few-to-no metrics measuring the independent effect of the nurse participation within the initiative. We don't know if this reflects the actual program realities, or merely how it is reported in the peer reviewed literature. There are currently no national or global measures available on nursing participation on ASPs and the metrics and incentives for including nurses remain undefined.

Through data charting we found that encouraging nurses to initiate discussion around proper antibiotic use is the most frequently used approach in hospital ASPs. One promising strategy reported appears to be the initiation of "timeouts", which have been identified by the CDC as effective antibiotic stewardship. These timeouts are designed facilitate the transition from broad-spectrum antibiotics, usually initiated empirically, to more targeted therapies, by having a structured discussion on antibiotic choice on at a designated point in time (e.g., the third calendar day of treatment).

Unfortunately, other CDC opportunities were identified less often, indicating gaps in evidence, and perhaps practice. In descending frequency, performing cultures correctly was a focus in three studies, optimizing testing was a focus in two, and assessing for a penicillin allergy was not a focus in any paper. This is a missed opportunity. Ten percent of patients report a penicillin allergy, but only 1% of the population is actually allergic. Improved evaluations for penicillin allergies have the potential to both lower costs and improve outcomes. Antibiotics for patients with penicillin allergies cost between 63% and 158% more than for those without an allergy. One healthcare system saw a savings of $2 million when it began assessing for penicillin allergies more rigorously. Further, patients who report a penicillin allergy often have longer hospital stays, which may be due in part to unnecessary exposure to antibiotics associated with Clostridium difficile and vancomycin-resistant enterococcus.

Despite these findings, it is important to acknowledge the limitations of the studies addressing this emerging field of inquiry and included in this review. Many of the interventions were relatively short in duration, 1 - 15 months, or did not publish details on duration and by nature of design we cannot infer these interventions will lend to sustainable practice change. In addition, half of the interventions were primarily aimed at the individual, such as education or reflection, and education is a weaker intervention in terms of sustainable practice change compared to interventions that change the work and/or are at the system-level. Further, outcomes like knowledge, satisfaction, and empowerment are weaker measures compared to clinical process and outcome measures where the work of the nurse can be quantified in terms of the health and safety of the patient. These papers and this review has laid a foundation for future work to address the nature and duration of the interventions, issues of sustainability, and key process and outcome measures.
CONCLUSION

Hospital-based nurses are uniquely situated to make a substantive impact on reducing antibiotic resistance, not only for their individual patients but also for the broader population. The role of nurses in ASPs varies and includes leading specific interventions or having an engaged presence on an interdisciplinary team. This review shows promising impact in targeted opportunities to prompt antibiotic discussions, though negligible impact in opportunities to optimize testing, perform cultures correctly and improve penicillin allergy evaluations. Additionally, no national or global measurement for nurse participation and engagement in ASPs exists. Healthcare administrators and policy makers can leverage the role of the nurse more effectively through targeted and purposeful structure to positively impact patient safety and healthcare quality as it relates to antibiotic stewardship.

IMPLICATIONS

This scoping review demonstrates existing gaps in research for engaging nurses in hospital ASPs, namely in culturing/testing practices and penicillin allergy evaluation. It also highlights the contributions that nurses are currently making in ASPs globally and the potential for increasing impact with increasing engagement. Additionally, meaningful measurements of nurse-engagement in hospital-based ASPs are needed to fully understand the impact and potential for nursing measures to reduce antibiotic resistance.
